summary: The second letter to TIP users from BBN, following RFC 365. BBN planned a series of such letters to document TIP system changes before the TIP User's Guide could be revised. It explains some changes, including ones suggested by users, such as the protocol to login command.

plainLanguage.summary: A newsletter for people who use dial-in boxes. It tells them about changes before the printed book is updated.

questions: how to fix a hung tip connection
subtitle: The second letter to TIP users documenting system changes and known issues.

tldr.problem: TIP (Terminal IMP) users needed to understand recent system changes and known problems that the user guide could not yet document.
tldr.mechanism: BBN issued a series of letters to TIP users to communicate changes, including command modifications (LOGIN, HOST, TRANSMIT), UI improvements, and documentation of known issues like lost allocations and logger timeout problems.
tldr.outcome: TIP users learned about upcoming changes and received workarounds for connectivity problems caused by network partitions and incomplete transmissions.

sections.title: TIP Changes and Commands
sections.content: BBN sent its second letter to TIP users (RFC 365 was the first). These letters documented TIP system changes before the TIP User's Guide (TUG) could be revised. Command changes included removing @PROTOCOL TO LOGIN and @PROTOCOL TO CLOSE, which had been superseded by @LOGIN and @CLOSE. The @LOGIN command would soon take a host number as a parameter (previously given with @HOST), and @HOST would be changed to do both @RECEIVE FROM HOST and @SEND TO HOST simultaneously.
sections.plainLanguage: The new version of the dial-in software is changing how you type commands. Old commands are going away and new ones are coming.

sections.title: Network Issues and Workarounds
sections.content: The letter describes a problem where network partitions could leave a TIP and host with conflicting views of their connection. If the network partitioned while a user sent a message to an unreachable host, the TIP would type DEAD and close. But the host might not have noticed the partition and still thought it had an open connection. When the TIP tried to re-LOGIN, the host refused because it already had a socket open with that TIP device. Another related problem occurs when an IMP crashes and drops a message packet; the source gets an incomplete transmission message, and the TIP closes and declares the destination dead. The letter describes how to recover: users can execute the Host/Host protocol reset command (though it is undocumented and rather crude), or call the host to log out the hung job manually.
sections.plainLanguage: Sometimes when the network hiccups, a dial-in box and the computer think they are still talking when they are not. The letter explains how to fix it, though the fix is not pretty.

sections.title: Logger Timeout and Command Updates
sections.content: The logger (the part that handles login) has three phases: phase 1 is waiting to get the logger, phase 2 is the login sequence (only one user at a time), and phase 3 is waiting for the host to open data connections. A single user can tie up phase 2 for about one minute (the timeout). Abort Login (@A L) behaves differently depending on which phase the user is in. BBN also noted changes to @TRANSMIT commands: @TRANSMIT ON NO CHARACTERS and ON EVERY CHARACTER would be removed, and @TRANSMIT EVERY and @TRANSMIT ON LINEFEED would additionally send when the input buffer is almost full. The NEWS herald would be removed because BBN could not determine when everyone had read it. Finally, the DEVICE CODE EXECUPORT command would be renamed DEVICE CODE EXTRA-PADDING to cover other terminals that need the feature.
sections.plainLanguage: Logging in can be slow and confusing when many people try at once. Some commands are being redesigned to send data more often and to avoid unnecessary delays.
